headline: Dividend cut of nearly 50% triggered an 18% share price fall as retained profits or franking credits ran thin; cautionary tale for LIC income investors
reasoning: WAM Capital, the listed investment company run by Geoff Wilson, cut its dividend by almost half rather than gradually reducing it, causing the share price to fall approximately 18%. The speakers explain that LICs can pay dividends in excess of their underlying income by drawing on retained profits, but WAM Capital reached the limits of this practice. This is flagged as a risk inherent in LICs that offer high headline dividends.
quote: We had Harvey Norman come out, Wham Capital. So there was a big sell off in Wham Capital, one of the list investment companies, which is one of those risks they cut their dividend. The stock fell by 18% or thereabouts. As a list investment company, they can pay a higher dividend than the dividends they're bringing in, but they said they were running out of retained profits or Frank, whatever it happened to be. They've almost halved the dividend going forward as opposed to cutting it slowly and investors sold off pretty simple.

headline: Acknowledges dividend was grown too aggressively; should have taken conservative cuts earlier to preserve profit reserve, reducing reliance on high yield on assets
reasoning: Management conceded the board was too aggressive in raising the dividend during strong periods and should have taken a more conservative approach earlier, particularly during years when assets declined slightly. Had the dividend been cut by a couple of cents in prior difficult years, an additional 10 cents per share would remain in the profit reserve today, giving greater flexibility. The lesson taken is to be more conservative on the dividend growth lever going forward, with future increases tied more directly to underlying portfolio performance.

headline: Wilson acknowledges in retrospect that WAM Capital's dividend was set too high during COVID, which structurally impaired capital growth for shareholders
reasoning: During COVID, many companies cut dividends but WAM Capital chose to maintain its payout. With the portfolio falling 20% and a dividend yield of around 10%, shareholders effectively saw total returns drop 30% from which recovery was difficult. Wilson concedes the dividend was paying out too much relative to portfolio returns, making it mathematically impossible to deliver capital growth alongside a 10-11% grossed-up yield if total returns were only around 10%. The board has since focused on not growing dividends too quickly and monitoring profit reserves.
quote: With WAM Capital being the prime example, we had gone too hard on the dividend. We were paying too high a dividend out to you as a shareholder, which you're getting, say, 10% yield and of course the tax we pay on it, say 10 or 11% grossed up, then you can't expect to get, if we're only doing 10% prattums and we're giving you a 10% yield or 11% yield, you can't get capital growth as well. So to me with WAM Capital, the boards specifically decided we're gonna keep paying that high dividend until we can't and keep an eye on the profit reserve there.

headline: WAM Capital profit reserve still covers over a year of dividends but franking credits unlikely to return to 100% within two years
reasoning: WAM Capital currently has more than a year of profit reserve remaining. The board has consciously decided to maintain a high dividend (10-11% grossed up) even though this means paying out more than earned, effectively returning capital. Franking on dividends is currently at 60% rather than 100% due to tax losses on the balance sheet. Management indicated that carry-forward losses don't need to be fully recouped before franking resumes, but cautioned against expecting a rapid return to full franking, with a board member suggesting a gentle increase from 60% upwards rather than full franking within the next couple of years.
quote: So if you put your money in a trust or an ETF and it goes up 10%, then the value of the ETF goes up 10%. If you put your money in an LIC and the assets go up 10%, so the assets go up 10%, but then you pay tax, you pay 30% tax. So 3% you lose, so it's gone up 7%. Now, if you're then paying out a fully frank dividend of 7%, then there's no capital growth. You've got it all as a fully frank dividend. So, yeah, that's, and that's pretty much where with WAM, we're actually paying, we're paying more than what we're earning as dividends out. So we're effectively paying out capital. But to me, it's, the plan is, we are what we're trying to do and say, with income maximiser, with the various other ones is to have a reasonable dividend, but don't push it as high as, say 7% fully frank. You have it down around that 6%, so then there'll be a percent or two capital growth as well.
